subject: 왕가의 계곡 도굴의 역사
title: Robbing the royal tombs of an ancient valley
content: The valley on the west bank at Thebes holds the tombs of Egyptian rulers of the New Kingdom, cut deep into rock and sealed. Almost every one of them was emptied in antiquity, and the robbing began within a few generations of the burials, which makes the history of the theft nearly as old as the tombs themselves. Ancient records document it directly. Papyri from the twelfth century before our era record investigations into tomb robbery, with the names of accused men, the confessions extracted, and the disputes between officials about who was responsible. One text describes an inspection in which several royal tombs were found violated, and another records a court hearing where a stonemason described breaking through a wall. Few ancient civilizations left such a precise account of crimes against their own monuments. The response was organised. Priests of a later era gathered the surviving royal bodies, rewrapped them, and hid them together in two caches, one in a cliff shaft and one in a tomb, where they remained until the nineteenth century. When those caches were found, they contained the remains of many of the greatest rulers of the empire, moved and labelled by officials who had been trying to protect them. The single tomb found nearly intact was small, belonged to a ruler who died young, and had been overlooked because later construction buried its entrance. Even that tomb had been entered twice in antiquity and hastily resealed. Modern archaeology in the valley therefore studies a site that was systematically emptied three thousand years ago. What survives is the architecture, the painted walls, the discarded fragments, and the administrative record of the robberies, and reconstructing what the tombs originally held depends heavily on that last source.

subject: 원형 경기장의 관중 동선
title: Moving fifty thousand people through an ancient building
content: The great amphitheatre at Rome could hold something on the order of fifty thousand spectators, and the problem its builders solved was not structural but circulatory. Filling and emptying a building of that capacity quickly requires that crowds never meet head on, and the design of this ancient monument addresses that requirement throughout. Eighty arched entrances ring the ground level, numbered so that a ticket could direct a spectator to a particular arch. From there a system of stairs and vaulted corridors carried them upward and inward to an exit into the seating, and the routes were separated by tier, so that those bound for the upper levels never crossed the paths of those seated below. Rank determined which route a person used. Senators entered at ground level and sat closest to the arena; those of lower standing climbed further, and the highest tier, reserved for the poorest and for women, was reached by stairways that did not connect to the lower system at all. The architecture therefore enforced the hierarchy of the empire physically, and a spectator's whole experience of the building depended on where they belonged in it. Modern engineers have studied the arrangement and estimate that the structure could be emptied in a short time, which no comparable modern venue matches without the same principle. Contemporary stadium design uses the identical solution of separated tiers with dedicated vertical circulation, arrived at independently and rediscovered repeatedly. What the ruins record is a civilization that had solved a crowd management problem by the first century of our era and encoded its social order in the solution. The seating chart was a diagram of Roman society, and the corridors that kept the classes apart on the way in were as deliberate as the arena itself.

subject: 팔미라의 대상 무역
title: An ancient city that lived on the desert crossing
content: Palmyra stood in the Syrian desert at an oasis, roughly midway between the Mediterranean and the Euphrates, and it grew wealthy during the first three centuries of our era by organising the crossing. This was not a city that produced goods; it was a city that made a dangerous journey survivable, and its ancient monuments were paid for by that service. Inscriptions record how the system worked. Stone tablets honour individual caravan leaders by name, praising them for bringing a company through safely, for paying costs from their own funds, or for negotiating with tribes along the route. Such honours were voted by the civic council, so the surviving record of this civilization consists largely of the community thanking the men who ran its convoys. Almost no other ancient city left documentation of that kind. The tariff inscription is the most detailed single document. A long text set up in the second century lists charges for goods entering and leaving, itemising slaves, purple dye, olive oil, salt, and animals, and specifying the rates in local currency. It survives because a copy was carved in stone, and it supplies a level of administrative detail that few sites of the era preserve. The city's art records the same mixture. Funerary portraits combine Roman drapery, Parthian ornament, and inscriptions in the local Aramaic dialect alongside Greek, so the population's position between two empires appears on its tombs. Its independence ended in the third century when a ruler of the city challenged Rome and was defeated. The routes shifted, the population fell, and the colonnaded streets stood empty in the desert until European travellers arrived in the seventeenth century and began recording what remained.

subject: 흑사병이 지나간 경로
title: Mapping how a medieval plague moved
content: The plague that reached Europe in the middle of the fourteenth century can be traced with unusual precision, because it moved through a society that kept records. Wills, church registers, court rolls, and municipal accounts all break in a recognisable pattern as a district is struck, and historians have used those breaks to reconstruct the route across the medieval continent almost month by month. It arrived by sea. The first appearances are at ports, and the disease then moves inland along rivers and roads at a pace that matches the speed of ordinary travel rather than any faster spread. This pattern is itself evidence about transmission, since a disease carried by people and goods advances as fast as they do, and the medieval record shows exactly that. Some inland regions were reached months after the coast a short distance away. The mortality was uneven in ways that the sources make visible. Certain villages lost more than half their inhabitants while neighbours lost a fraction, and the difference frequently corresponds to whether a settlement lay on a route. A few remote districts escaped a given wave entirely and were struck by a later one. Ancient and medieval accounts of earlier epidemics allow comparison, and the sequence of recurrences over the following three centuries has been mapped as carefully as the first arrival. Recent work has added genetic evidence. Material recovered from burial pits of the era has yielded the organism itself, confirming the identification that historians had argued about, and comparison across sites in different countries has begun to show which waves were connected. The written record supplies the timing and the archaeology supplies the organism, and neither alone would have settled the questions that this catastrophe has raised for six centuries.

subject: 내륙 상인 조직의 연결망
title: Merchant lineages that ran an inland empire's commerce
content: During the later centuries of imperial China, several regional merchant groups organised themselves around lineage and native place, and their networks reached across the whole empire. Members from one prefecture would dominate a particular commodity, maintain halls in distant cities, and extend credit to one another across enormous distances without any enforceable contract between provinces. Their tool was the native place hall. A hall built in a far city served traders from one home region, giving them beds, storage, a judge for quarrels, and a temple, and joining it turned on where a man came from rather than on any deal he had struck. So a trader reaching a strange city found a body that would vouch for him, and one who cheated was shut out of a web he could not rebuild. Good name did the work that no court would do. The historical record of these bodies is unusually good. Halls kept minutes, noted gifts, and cut the names of donors into stone, and thousands of these carved records survive across the empire. From them historians have worked out which regions dealt in which wares, how far the webs reached, and how they shifted across several centuries. Family records, printed by the lineages themselves, supply a second line of proof. What the case illustrates about the era is how commerce functioned in an empire whose formal legal institutions were not designed for it. The imperial office cared about land and grain, so far reaching trade grew its own means of trust, built from kin and home place rather than from law. When the empire fell and the halls shut, the ties beneath them held, and several great trading families of the next century came straight from these lines.

subject: 조선 실록의 보관 방식
title: An archive copied four times and hidden in mountains
content: The Joseon dynasty maintained a court record covering roughly five centuries, compiled after each ruler's death from the daily notes of official historians. What makes this archive notable is less what it says than how it was kept, since the same historical record was copied in four sets and held in stores placed far apart on purpose. The reasoning was explicit. One store can burn, and the dynasty had learned this when an invasion late in the sixteenth century destroyed three of the four, leaving a single set from which the rest were made again. After that the copies were moved to mountain sites chosen for being far off rather than handy, watched by nearby temples, and checked on a fixed round. Access was restricted absolutely. Reigning rulers were not permitted to read the record of their own reign, which was the arrangement that made the historians' notes worth keeping, since an official who could be overruled would have written differently. Accounts of the era describe rulers asking to read the entries and being refused, and the refusals were themselves written down. Maintenance was continuous. Volumes were aired now and then against damp and insects, wrapped in cloth, and kept in cases, and the check lists note the state of each set. Such care across centuries needed a body that outlived single reigns, and that is the real feat. The record lasted into the twentieth century, although the sets were scattered under colonial rule and one was largely lost to fire abroad. What remains is among the longest continuous historical records produced by any civilization, and its survival was not luck but the result of a policy adopted after a catastrophe and maintained by people who never saw the whole span they were protecting.

subject: 류큐 왕국의 중계 무역
title: An island kingdom that lived between empires
content: The Ryukyu kingdom occupied a chain of small islands between Japan, China, and south east Asia, with almost no land suitable for producing a surplus. From the fourteenth to the sixteenth century it nevertheless supported a court, built stone fortresses, and maintained embassies abroad, and it did so by carrying goods between others. The arrangement depended on a diplomatic position. The kingdom entered the tributary system of the Ming empire, which granted it trading rights and regular missions to the Chinese court, and at the same time it dealt with Japan and with kingdoms further south. Because the Ming had restricted private maritime commerce, an authorised intermediary became extremely valuable, and this small kingdom occupied that role for roughly two centuries. Its ships carried Chinese silk and ceramics south, brought back pepper, sappanwood, and aromatics, and moved Japanese silver and swords into the same circuit. An inscription cast on a palace bell in the fifteenth century describes the kingdom as a bridge between nations, and the claim was commercial rather than merely rhetorical. The court kept records of these missions, and the surviving diplomatic correspondence documents dealings with a dozen states. Decline followed changes elsewhere. When the Ming restrictions eased and European vessels entered the same waters, the intermediary's advantage disappeared, and an invasion from a Japanese domain in the early seventeenth century left the kingdom paying tribute in two directions at once. It survived in that condition until it was annexed in the nineteenth century. What the case demonstrates about the era is that position could substitute for resources. A civilization with no exportable surplus prospered for two hundred years because of where its islands lay and what the surrounding empires had forbidden.

subject: 마자파힛의 해상 지배
title: A medieval empire held together by ships
content: The Majapahit empire, centred on eastern Java during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, claimed authority over an enormous area of islands and coasts. Reconstructing what that authority actually amounted to has occupied historians for a long time, since a maritime empire leaves a different record from a territorial one. The principal source is a court poem composed in the fourteenth century, which lists the territories acknowledging the ruler and describes a royal progress through the countryside. Its catalogue names places across the archipelago and beyond, and taking it literally would give the empire a reach comparable to a modern state. Most historians now read the list as a claim about prestige and tribute rather than administration, since no machinery for governing such distances existed. Archaeology supplies a different kind of evidence. Excavation at the capital has revealed a planned settlement with brick structures, water tanks, and canals, along with enormous quantities of imported Chinese ceramics, which confirms the wealth that the poem asserts. Coins from the era circulated widely, and their distribution maps commercial reach even where political control is doubtful. What held the arrangement together was control of choke points. Ships moving between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea passed through a small number of straits, and a power able to tax or to threaten that traffic gained income without governing any hinterland. This is a recurring pattern in the history of maritime states. The empire declined during the fifteenth century as coastal ports converted to Islam and asserted independence, and by the early sixteenth it had fragmented. Its memory persisted, and later states in the region invoked it as a precedent, which is why arguments about how large it actually was have carried political weight long after the civilization itself ended.

subject: 잉카 도로망의 관리
title: Roads without wheels across an ancient empire
content: The Inca empire built and maintained a road system covering tens of thousands of kilometres, running the length of the Andes and along the coast, connecting territories that stretched across a distance comparable to the whole of Europe. It was constructed for people and llamas rather than for vehicles, since this ancient civilization used no wheeled transport, and the engineering reflects that fact throughout. Steep ground was climbed by stone stairways rather than by switchbacks, since a walking party can take steps that a cart cannot. Suspension bridges of woven fibre crossed gorges, and each was rebuilt annually by the communities on either side as a labour obligation to the state. One such bridge is still remade each year using the same technique, which makes it among the few pieces of ancient infrastructure anywhere kept in service by its original method. Way stations stood along the routes at intervals, stocked with food, cloth, and equipment, and the surrounding population supplied them as part of their tribute. Runners carried messages in relay between posts, and accounts from the century of the conquest describe news travelling hundreds of kilometres in a day. The empire had no writing, so the runners carried knotted cords and memorised messages. Maintenance was itself the tribute. Communities owed labour rather than goods, and repairing the section of road passing their territory was among the obligations recorded, so the network existed because the administration could command work across an enormous area. What the roads finally record is therefore an organisational achievement rather than a technical one. The surfaces and bridges were within the capacity of any settled society; commanding the coordinated labour of millions of people across mountains for a century was not, and the empire's collapse left the roads intact and the arrangement that maintained them gone.

subject: 이누이트의 겨울 주거
title: Building shelter where nothing grows
content: Peoples living in the far north built winter dwellings from the only materials at hand, and the results are among the more instructive cases in the study of how human cultures adapt. In much of the ancient Arctic there is no timber, no thatch, and no workable stone for part of the year, so shelter had to be made from snow, from earth, and from the bones and skins of animals. The snow house is the best known. Blocks cut from firm drifted snow are laid in a rising spiral, each course leaning inward, so the structure closes itself without any support during construction. The shape is not a hemisphere but a catenary curve, which is the form that carries its own weight most efficiently, and builders arrived at it by practice rather than by calculation. A skilled pair could raise one in about an hour. Its performance depends on physics that the builders understood in practical terms. Snow is a poor conductor, so body heat and a small lamp raise the interior temperature far above the outside air, and a sleeping platform built higher than the entrance keeps the warm air where people lie while cold air settles into the sunken passage. A small vent prevents the interior glazing over. Other winter dwellings across the region were semi subterranean, framed with driftwood or whale bone and roofed with turf, and archaeology has recovered many such structures, some occupied over long periods. The choice between forms depended on whether a community moved with the ice or stayed at a coastal site. What these buildings demonstrate is knowledge accumulated across generations without any written record. Every element solves a specific problem of the environment, and the solutions were transmitted by building alongside somebody who already knew, which is how most technical knowledge in history has actually travelled.

subject: 은이 돈 세계의 순환
title: The metal that linked four continents
content: During the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries an enormous quantity of silver was extracted from mines in the Americas, and most of it did not stay there. Historians tracing where it went have reconstructed a circuit that connected the Americas, Europe, and Asia, and this early modern flow is among the clearest demonstrations that a genuinely global exchange existed centuries before the term was invented. The metal moved because it was worth more in one place than another. China had converted its tax system to silver payment, so demand there was enormous and the ratio between silver and gold differed sharply from European levels. Consequently silver carried east bought more than it did at home, and merchants moved it in both directions around the world: across the Atlantic to Europe and onward through the Levant, and directly across the Pacific from the American coast to Manila and thence to China. The mining itself rested on forced labour. A rotational draft obliged indigenous communities to supply workers to the mountain mines, and mortality there was severe, so the metal that financed empires and reordered exchange across the world was produced under conditions that contemporary observers described with alarm. Any account of this era that follows only the metal misses that fact entirely. The consequences reached everywhere. Prices in Europe rose across the century in a way that contemporaries could not explain, states that controlled the mines borrowed against future shipments and defaulted repeatedly, and the eventual reduction of the flow contributed to fiscal crises across several empires. Historians still argue about how much of the century's disruption should be attributed to this single commodity, and the argument continues because the evidence is genuinely mixed rather than because the connection is doubted.

subject: 대서양 삼각 항로의 항구
title: Port towns built by a crossing that carried people
content: Between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries, ships crossed the Atlantic in a circuit that carried manufactured goods south, enslaved people west, and plantation produce back north. Historians rebuild this era from the records the traffic itself made. Ships were insured, taxed, and listed, and those papers survive in bulk. Ports on several coasts were rebuilt by the proceeds. Warehouses, docks, and trading houses in several European cities date from this era. The bodies founded there — banks, insurance offices, and exchanges — grew from the need to fund voyages of more than a year and to spread the risk of loss. Municipal buildings, hospitals, and endowed schools in the same cities carry the names of families whose wealth came from this circuit. On the African coast, walled posts were built and rebuilt across three centuries. Archaeology at these sites has recorded the holding rooms and the towns around them that fed and served them. The ties between the coastal states and the arriving ships were both trading and political rather than simple, and recent historical work has fixed on exactly those ties. The largest record project in the field has gathered accounts of tens of thousands of single voyages, taken from port books, customs papers, and ship lists held in a dozen countries. From these one can state the scale of the traffic, how it rose and fell, and the routes taken, with an exactness that earlier historians simply did not have. What that record establishes is a matter of numbers rather than of impression. Roughly twelve million people were carried, a substantial fraction did not survive the crossing, and the demographic consequences for the regions involved are visible in every subsequent century.

subject: 오스만 예니체리 제도
title: An imperial corps raised from conquered households
content: The Ottoman empire maintained a standing infantry corps at a time when European rulers depended on feudal levies and hired companies. Its members were recruited by a system that took boys from Christian villages within the empire, converted them, trained them, and bound them to the ruler personally, and the arrangement lasted in some form for roughly four centuries. The recruits were legally the ruler's property and could hold no ordinary family ties, which was the point. A soldier with no lineage, no land, and no local patron owed everything to the palace, so the corps supplied a force that no provincial magnate could suborn. Training was long, discipline was severe, and the resulting infantry was among the most effective in the medieval and early modern world. The system produced administrators as well as soldiers. Boys assessed as capable were educated in the palace school in languages, law, and administration, and several rose to the highest offices of the empire. Consequently the ruling elite of this civilization was drawn substantially from people who had begun as village children in conquered provinces, which is an arrangement with few parallels in the history of any state. Its later development inverted the original design. Members began to marry, to enrol their sons, and to engage in trade, and by the seventeenth century the corps had become a hereditary interest with its own politics, capable of deposing rulers rather than serving them. Several attempts at reform were defeated by the corps itself. It was finally destroyed by force in 1826, after the empire's rulers concluded that no reform of the army was possible while it existed. Historians have used the whole sequence as a case study in how an institution designed to prevent a particular danger can become that danger across a few generations.

subject: 네덜란드 간척지의 마을
title: Villages on ground taken from the water
content: Much of the northern Netherlands lies below sea level, and the settlements there stand on land that was created rather than found. The process began in the medieval centuries and continued for eight hundred years, and the historical record of it is unusually complete because reclaiming ground required institutions that kept documents. The earliest method was drainage by ditch. Peat bogs were cut with parallel channels, water ran off, and the ground could be farmed, and the long narrow fields that resulted still define the landscape. Drained peat compacts and sinks, however, so ground reclaimed in one century lay below the water table in the next, and the same communities had to build dikes to keep out the water they had originally released. Windmills lifting water into raised channels solved the problem from the fifteenth century onward, and larger schemes followed. Lakes were surrounded by a ring dike and a ring canal and then pumped dry by mills working in series, each lifting water part of the way, and the resulting basins were divided into rectangular holdings and settled. Several such projects were financed by investors from the cities, so the villages laid out in them are among the earliest planned rural settlements in Europe. What made the arrangement durable was the water board. Landholders in a drained district were obliged to maintain the works and elected officials to enforce it, and these bodies levied charges, held courts, and predate most other institutions of the country. They still exist. Historians of this era treat them as an unusually clear case of collective management, since the alternative to cooperation was that everybody's fields flooded together. The landscape therefore records a civilization organised around a permanent obligation, and abandoning maintenance for even a few years would return much of the country to water.

subject: 19세기 파리의 도시 개조
title: Cutting new streets through an old city
content: Between 1853 and 1870 the ancient centre of Paris was rebuilt. Broad avenues were cut through districts of narrow medieval lanes, thousands of buildings were pulled down, and a single style of frontage was imposed along these new routes. The project was directed by a prefect acting under the authority of the emperor, and it remains among the most drastic transformations any European capital has undergone. Several motives operated together, although only some of them were stated. The old centre was crowded and repeatedly struck by epidemic disease, so the new sewers, water supply, and wider streets addressed a genuine sanitary emergency that historians of the era document thoroughly. Circulation was also a concern, since goods and people could not move through a street plan inherited from earlier centuries. A third motive was political, and contemporaries said so openly: such wide straight avenues are hard to barricade and easy for troops to cross, and this city had seen repeated risings. Because these works were expensive, their social consequences were severe, and they were understood at the time. Poorer residents of the demolished districts could not afford the new buildings and moved outward, so the rebuilding sorted the population by income in a way the older city had not. Critics of the era described the process as expulsion dressed as improvement, and the argument has continued in every subsequent city that attempted something similar. This visual result became a model for the century that followed. Other capitals copied its avenues, its uniform cornice line, and its diagonal vistas ending in a monument, and the style was carried to colonial cities across several continents. What this century of rebuilding demonstrates is how completely a state can remake a city when it controls both the law and the finance, and how the resulting form outlives every argument that produced it.

subject: 초기 공장의 하루
title: What a working day became in the first mills
content: The textile mills of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries changed not only how goods were made but how time was experienced by those making them. Historians studying this era have found that the reorganisation of the working day was as significant as any change in machinery, and the surviving records document it closely. Earlier work had followed the task. A weaver at home worked intensely when an order was due and rested afterwards, and agricultural labour followed the season and the weather. The mill required something different, since machinery driven by a single water wheel or engine ran continuously and every hand had to be present at the same moment. Consequently attendance replaced completion as the measure of work. Enforcement was elaborate. Rule books from the era set out fines for lateness, for talking, for opening a window, and for leaving a workplace without permission, and the schedules of fines survive in company records. Clocks were installed and in some documented cases adjusted, and workers who owned watches were suspected of checking the employer's timekeeping. Disputes about time appear repeatedly in the records of the period. The hours themselves were extreme by any earlier standard, and the employment of children was widespread, which produced the parliamentary inquiries whose testimony forms one of the richest sources for daily life in that century. Witnesses describe the working day directly, and their evidence was gathered precisely because reformers wanted the record. What the era finally established was a habit that outlasted the mills. Working to a schedule set by somebody else, measured by a clock rather than by the task, became normal across an enormous range of occupations, and most people now organise their days by an arrangement that a few generations found alien enough to resist.

subject: 철도가 바꾼 시간 관념
title: When every town gave up its own noon
content: Before railways, each town kept its own time, set by the sun at that place. Noon in one city occurred several minutes later than in another to its east, and nobody found this inconvenient, because no activity required the two to agree. The railway made the arrangement unworkable, and the resolution of that problem across the nineteenth century changed how a whole civilization measured its days. Timetables were the immediate difficulty. A train leaving one town at a stated hour and arriving at another where the clocks read differently produced schedules that nobody could interpret, and collisions on single track lines followed directly from the confusion. Companies responded by adopting the time of their headquarters across the whole network, so a station clock might show railway time alongside local time, sometimes with two minute hands. Standardisation followed. Countries adopted a single national time, in several cases after decades of local resistance, since a town giving up its own noon was accepting that its clocks would be set elsewhere. Municipal authorities in a number of places refused for years. The international system of zones, agreed at a conference in the 1880s, extended the same logic across the world and required a decision about where the day should begin. The deeper change concerned habits. Punctuality measured against a public clock became a virtue in this era rather than a technicality, employers and schools organised themselves around it, and the pocket watch spread through the population. Historians of the century treat the railway as the instrument through which an abstract, uniform time replaced a time that had been local, natural, and slightly different in every place, and few changes in the history of ordinary life have been so complete or so rarely noticed afterwards.

subject: 상하수도와 전염병의 퇴조
title: The century when cities stopped killing their inhabitants
content: For most of history, large cities did not sustain their own populations. Deaths exceeded births, and the numbers held up only through continuous migration from the countryside, a pattern that historians can trace in parish registers across several centuries. During the nineteenth century this reversed in one European city after another, and the reversal is among the more consequential changes of that era. Epidemic disease was the immediate cause of the older pattern. Cholera arrived in Europe in the 1830s and struck repeatedly, and its investigation produced the celebrated study in which a physician mapped cases around a single water pump and argued that the disease travelled in water rather than in air. The argument was resisted for years, since the prevailing theory attributed such outbreaks to foul smells, and the two explanations happened to recommend some of the same measures. What followed was construction on an enormous scale. Cities built intercepting sewers, filtered and later treated their water supplies, and rebuilt districts to admit light and air, and the works were financed by municipal borrowing on a scale that had no precedent. The great sewer system of London, built after a summer in which the river became intolerable, is the best documented example, and comparable projects followed across the continent and beyond. The demographic effect is visible in the records. Mortality fell steeply in the decades following such works, and the fall preceded any effective treatment for the diseases involved, which is why historians of medicine emphasise engineering rather than clinical advance when accounting for this period. What the century established is that the health of a population depended on infrastructure maintained collectively, a conclusion that had to be reached against considerable resistance and at very great expense.

subject: 금광 정착지의 형성
title: Towns that appeared in a year and vanished in five
content: Discoveries of gold in the nineteenth century produced settlements that grew from nothing to thousands of inhabitants within months. Historians of these episodes have unusually good evidence, since the participants wrote letters, newspapers were founded almost immediately, and administrations arrived to record claims, so the whole life cycle of a town can be documented from its first week. The population arrived faster than any institution. In the earliest phase there was no court, no registry, and no police, and the miners themselves adopted rules in public meetings covering the size of a claim, how it must be worked to be held, and what would happen to a thief. Such codes were written down, and copies survive from many camps, showing rules that are strikingly similar across sites that had no contact, which suggests that participants brought expectations with them rather than inventing from nothing. Very few of those who came grew rich from mining. The surviving accounts show that the reliable money was in supply — transport, tools, food, and lodging — and prices in these settlements were extraordinary, so a great deal of what the diggings produced ended up with merchants rather than with miners. Several substantial commercial fortunes of the era began this way. The consequences for existing inhabitants were severe. Indigenous populations in each of the affected regions lost land and were subjected to violence documented in the contemporary record, and the historical scholarship of recent decades has concentrated on this dimension after a long period in which it was treated as background. Most of the settlements were abandoned within a decade. What remains is a landscape of workings and foundations, along with an archive that lets historians examine how a society organises itself when several thousand strangers arrive somewhere with no authority present.

subject: 층위학이라는 원리
title: The idea that made archaeology a discipline
content: The principle that underlies all excavation is simple to state: where layers of deposit lie undisturbed, the lower ones were laid down before the upper ones. Everything that archaeology says about sequence rests on this, and recognising it converted the digging up of ancient objects into a method capable of producing history. The idea came from geology. Nineteenth century observers of rock strata established that layers record time, and archaeologists applied the same reasoning to the accumulated deposits of human occupation, where floors, collapse, rubbish, and rebuilding pile up in the same way. A mound formed by a settlement occupied for millennia is a stack of such layers, and reading it in order supplies a relative chronology without any dating method whatever. Complications arise constantly. A pit dug in a later century cuts through earlier layers and fills with later material, so an object may lie physically low while belonging high in the sequence. Foundations, graves, and animal burrows all disturb the record, and identifying such intrusions is the central skill of excavation. Recording is therefore as important as digging, since the relationships between deposits vanish the moment they are removed. The method's power is that it works on relative order alone. Long before radiocarbon dating existed, archaeologists had built detailed sequences for whole regions by combining stratification at many sites with the changing styles of pottery found in each layer, and those sequences largely survived the arrival of absolute dating. What the principle finally established is that an ancient site is a document rather than a source of objects. Excavating carelessly destroys the sequence while recovering the artefacts, which is why the early treasure hunts at famous sites are now regarded as losses despite everything they produced.

subject: 나무 나이테로 읽는 연대
title: Counting rings to date a building
content: A tree adds one growth ring each year, and the width of that ring depends on the conditions of the season. Wet years produce wide rings and dry years narrow ones, so a cross section carries a record of the climate through the tree's life, and this fact supports one of the most precise dating methods available to archaeology and history. This technique works by matching patterns. A sequence of rings from a living tree overlaps with a sequence from an older timber, and that timber overlaps with something older still, so a chain can be built backwards for thousands of years within a region. Once such a master sequence exists, a piece of wood of unknown age can be matched against it, and although other methods give a range, this one gives a specific year, and in favourable cases the season in which the tree was felled. Its applications to historical questions are considerable. Roof timbers date a building, panels date a painting, and piles date a bridge, in each case supplying a year that documents may not record. Several disputes about the chronology of ancient and medieval structures have been settled this way, and because its evidence is physical, the method has overturned dates accepted for centuries on documentary grounds. Yet its limitations are real. It requires wood preserved with enough rings to match, it works only within a region where a master sequence has been built, and reused timber dates its own felling rather than the structure it now supports. Dating a beam therefore establishes the earliest possible date for a building rather than the actual one. These rings also record events beyond the local season. Very narrow rings appearing across a whole continent in the same year point to a volcanic eruption or a comparable disturbance, and historians have used such signals to date catastrophes that written sources describe only vaguely.

subject: 동위원소가 알려주는 이동
title: Reading a person's travels from their teeth
content: The chemistry of the ground varies from place to place, and what a person drinks and eats carries that signature into their body. Teeth form in childhood and then change very little, so the enamel of an adult preserves a record of where they lived when they were young, and this fact has transformed how archaeologists study movement in the ancient world. Two elements do most of this work. One varies with the age of the underlying rock, so a chalk region gives a different value from a granite one; the other varies with distance from the sea and with climate. Together they narrow the possible region of childhood considerably, and therefore comparing a person's teeth with the ground where they were buried shows whether they died where they grew up. These results have overturned assumptions repeatedly. Cemeteries once assumed to hold settled local populations turn out to contain substantial proportions of people raised elsewhere, sometimes at great distance. Individuals buried in prominent graves at famous ancient monuments have proved to be incomers, and communities that historians described as static have turned out to be mobile across generations. This method has also complicated old debates about whether a cultural change reflected migration or imitation, because it can answer that question for individuals. Although the technique is powerful, its limitations matter. The signature identifies regions with similar geology rather than a specific place, so several candidate origins usually remain, and diet complicates the reading where somebody ate imported food. Cremation destroys such evidence entirely, and that removes whole populations from study. What the technique has established beyond dispute is that ancient populations moved far more than the older picture allowed. Nearly every large study finds incomers, and the settled village of unchanging families that dominated earlier accounts of prehistory now looks like an assumption rather than a finding.

subject: 항공 사진이 찾아낸 유적
title: Sites that only appear from above
content: A buried ditch or wall changes the ground above it in ways that are invisible at eye level and obvious from the air. Crops growing over a filled ditch have deeper soil and more water, so they grow taller and ripen later; crops over buried masonry are stunted. These differences produce marks that appear from a height as clear outlines of structures nobody knew were there. The discovery was made by military fliers early in the twentieth century and developed into a method between the wars. Archaeologists flying over familiar countryside began recording enclosures, field systems, roads, and settlements in enormous numbers, and whole categories of ancient monument were identified for the first time. Some regions turned out to hold ten times as many sites as ground survey had found. The marks appear only under particular conditions. A dry summer stresses crops enough for the difference to show, so an exceptional season reveals sites that remain invisible for decades, and photographs taken in such years are consulted long afterwards. Light at a low angle reveals earthworks too slight to notice from the ground, which is why flights are made early and late in the day. Recent decades have added laser survey from aircraft, which measures the ground surface through vegetation and has revealed extensive ancient settlement under forest in several regions of the world, including areas assumed to have been uninhabited. The results in Central America and in Amazonia have substantially revised estimates of ancient population. What these methods share is that they find rather than excavate. A photograph or a scan shows where something lies without disturbing it, and given that excavation destroys what it examines, the ability to map a landscape without digging has been among the more valuable developments in the discipline.

subject: 실험 고고학의 방법
title: Learning about the past by making it again
content: When archaeologists want to know how an ancient object was made or used, one available method is to make one and use it. Experimental work of this kind has become a recognised part of the discipline, and it answers questions that no amount of examining the original artefact can settle. The technique addresses questions of process. A flint tool shows the scars of its manufacture, and knapping a replica establishes which sequence of blows produces those scars and which does not, so the traces on ancient tools become readable. Similar work has reconstructed how bronze was cast, how pots were fired, and how heavy stones might have been moved, and in each case the experiment narrows what is possible rather than proving what occurred. Use wear studies extend the method. Replicas are employed for a controlled period on a specified material — cutting hide, scraping wood, harvesting grain — and the resulting microscopic polish is compared with the wear on excavated tools. This has established what many ancient implements were actually used for, which their shape alone does not reveal. Longer projects test whole systems. Reconstructed houses have been built and inhabited, ancient crops grown with period tools on measured plots, and vessels built to excavated designs sailed across open water. The reconstructed field plots in particular have produced yield figures that feed directly into estimates of how many people a given ancient landscape could support. The method's discipline lies in its limits. An experiment shows that something could have been done in a particular way, never that it was, and a modern person working with replicas lacks the lifetime of practice an ancient specialist possessed. Good experimental work states these limits explicitly, and its value lies in eliminating explanations rather than in confirming any single one.
